slides.body: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery.
You need two things from earlier in the course.

skip a commit that cannot be tested, and read what Git reports then;
read the bisect state from its refs and its log, and end the session cleanly.

slides.body: In one sentence: 🟡 CAUTION, git bisect finds the commit that changed a property by checking out a commit in the middle of the suspects, asking you for a verdict, and halving the suspects until one is left.
The label is CAUTION and not SAFE because bisect detaches HEAD and checks out other commits into your working tree, and it writes refs and files into .git.

slides.body: When to use it: when reading gives no suspect, or several.
One more requirement. Bisect needs commits that can be tested one by one.
Now a picture to keep. The textbook's analogy is looking up a word in a printed dictionary.
The analogy breaks in two places, and both are where bisections go wrong.
First, history is a graph, not a list.

items: Marking a commit that crashes as "bad". Root cause: a verdict is a statement about one property, and a crash for another reason is "no verdict"; the false statement sends the search into the wrong half.
Starting a bisection with uncommitted changes. Root cause: Git refuses to check out the next commit over uncommitted changes to files it has to replace.

Trusting the result when the bug came and went. Root cause: bisect assumes a single transition from good to bad and cannot detect that the property is not monotonic; test the reported commit and its parent yourself.

Skipping commits next to the culprit and expecting one answer. Root cause: the manual states that if you skip a commit adjacent to the one you are looking for, Git cannot tell which of them was the first bad one, and it ends with a list of candidates.
Forgetting git bisect reset. Root cause: until the reset, HEAD is detached, and commits made in that state belong to no branch.

beats.text: In the previous video you answered this by reading commits, the saved snapshots of the project. You guessed that the fault was in normalization, you blamed the function, you looked through the formatter. That worked because you had an idea of where to look.
beats.tele: In the previous video you answered this by reading commits, the saved snapshots of the project. You guessed that the fault was in normalization, you blamed the function, you looked through the formatter. That worked because you had an idea of where to look.

beats.text: Now remove the idea. The fault is in a file nobody suspects, or the diff between the last good release and today is four thousand commits by sixty people. Reading doesn't scale. What you do have is a test: one command that says yes or no. With a test and two endpoints, Git can find the commit in about twelve steps for four thousand commits, without you understanding the code at all.

beats.text: In one sentence: 🟡 CAUTION, git bisect finds the commit that changed a property by checking out a commit in the middle of the suspects, asking you for a verdict, and halving the suspects until one is left.
beats.tele: In one sentence: 🟡 CAUTION, `git bisect` finds the commit that changed a property by checking out a commit in the middle of the suspects, asking you for a verdict, and halving the suspects until one is left.

beats.text: The label is CAUTION and not SAFE because bisect detaches HEAD and checks out other commits into your working tree, and it writes refs and files into .git. A ref is a name that holds a commit ID. It's recoverable with one command, git bisect reset.
beats.tele: The label is CAUTION and not SAFE because bisect detaches HEAD and checks out other commits into your working tree, and it writes refs and files into `.git`. A ref is a name that holds a commit ID. It's recoverable with one command, `git bisect reset`.

beats.text: Precisely. You give one commit that has the property, called "bad" or "new", and at least one ancestor, an earlier commit in its history, that lacks it, called "good" or "old". The candidates are the commits reachable from the bad one and not from any good one.
beats.tele: Precisely. You give one commit that has the property, called "bad" or "new", and at least one ancestor, an earlier commit in its history, that lacks it, called "good" or "old". The candidates are the commits reachable from the bad one and not from any good one.

beats.text: That's a range, the same two-dot range you already know. Git assumes there is a single first bad commit: in the manual's words, "all its descendants are 'bad' and all the other commits are 'good'". At each step it picks the candidate that splits the remaining candidates most evenly.
beats.tele: That's a range, the same two-dot range you already know. Git assumes there is a single first bad commit: in the manual's words, "all its descendants are 'bad' and all the other commits are 'good'". At each step it picks the candidate that splits the remaining candidates most evenly.

beats.text: The arithmetic. Every verdict halves the candidates. So k verdicts can separate two to the power k candidates, and N candidates need about log2 of N verdicts.
beats.tele: The arithmetic. Every verdict halves the candidates. So k verdicts can separate two to the power k candidates, and N candidates need about log2 of N verdicts.

beats.text: Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: start from 4,000 and keep halving until one is left. Count the halvings, then say your answer.
beats.tele: Try it now, on paper. Thirty seconds: start from 4,000 and keep halving until one is left. Count the halvings, then say your answer.

beats.text: About twelve. That's the number from the opening.
beats.tele: About twelve. That's the number from the opening.

beats.text: Doubling the history adds one test. This is why "it worked in the last release" is enough of a starting point, however long ago that was.
beats.tele: Doubling the history adds one test. This is why "it worked in the last release" is enough of a starting point, however long ago that was.

beats.text: Inside .git, a bisection is state, kept until you end it. Every verdict is a ref under refs/bisect/. A file BISECT_START holds where to return to, BISECT_TERMS holds the two words in use, and BISECT_LOG holds the session so far.
beats.tele: Inside `.git`, a bisection is state, kept until you end it. Every verdict is a ref under `refs/bisect/`. A file `BISECT_START` holds where to return to, `BISECT_TERMS` holds the two words in use, and `BISECT_LOG` holds the session so far.

beats.text: When to use it: when reading gives no suspect, or several. When not to: don't bisect what you can read. If the pickaxe or blame names one commit, and a test at that commit and its parent confirms it, you're done. And don't bisect before you have checked that the known-good commit is still good in today's environment. If the cause is a dependency that floated to a new version, or a data file outside Git, every commit may be bad and bisect will report whatever the noise selects.

If the pickaxe or blame names one commit, and a test at that commit and its parent confirms it, you're done. And don't bisect before you have checked that the known-good commit is still good in today's environment. If the cause is a dependency that floated to a new version, or a data file outside Git, every commit may be bad and bisect will report whatever the noise selects.

beats.text: One more requirement. Bisect needs commits that can be tested one by one. A history of small commits that each build gives an answer you can read in a minute. A history of large squashes gives an answer that is a two-thousand-line diff.
beats.tele: One more requirement. Bisect needs commits that can be tested one by one. A history of small commits that each build gives an answer you can read in a minute. A history of large squashes gives an answer that is a two-thousand-line diff.

beats.text: Now a picture to keep. The textbook's analogy is looking up a word in a printed dictionary. Open in the middle, see whether your word comes before or after, repeat with that half.

beats.text: The analogy breaks in two places, and both are where bisections go wrong.
beats.tele: The analogy breaks in two places, and both are where bisections go wrong.

beats.text: First, history is a graph, not a list. "The middle" has to be computed. With a merge in the range, a commit that joins two lines of work, the commit Git picks isn't the one you would pick by counting lines of git log.
beats.tele: First, history is a graph, not a list. "The middle" has to be computed. With a merge in the range, a commit that joins two lines of work, the commit Git picks isn't the one you would pick by counting lines of `git log`.

beats.text: Second, a dictionary is sorted by construction. "Good before, bad after" is an assumption about your project, and bisect can't verify it. If the bug was introduced, fixed and introduced again, there is more than one first bad commit. Bisect finds one transition and can't tell you there are others.
beats.tele: Second, a dictionary is sorted by construction. "Good before, bad after" is an assumption about your project, and bisect can't verify it. If the bug was introduced, fixed and introduced again, there is more than one first bad commit. Bisect finds one transition and can't tell you there are others.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Marking a commit that crashes as "bad". Root cause: a verdict is a statement about one property, and a crash for another reason is "no verdict"; the false statement sends the search into the wrong half.
beats.tele: Marking a commit that crashes as "bad". Root cause: a verdict is a statement about one property, and a crash for another reason is "no verdict"; the false statement sends the search into the wrong half.

beats.text: Starting a bisection with uncommitted changes. Root cause: Git refuses to check out the next commit over uncommitted changes to files it has to replace.
beats.tele: Starting a bisection with uncommitted changes. Root cause: Git refuses to check out the next commit over uncommitted changes to files it has to replace.

beats.text: Trusting the result when the bug came and went. Root cause: bisect assumes a single transition from good to bad and cannot detect that the property is not monotonic; test the reported commit and its parent yourself.
beats.tele: Trusting the result when the bug came and went. Root cause: bisect assumes a single transition from good to bad and cannot detect that the property is not monotonic; test the reported commit and its parent yourself.

beats.text: Skipping commits next to the culprit and expecting one answer. Root cause: the manual states that if you skip a commit adjacent to the one you are looking for, Git cannot tell which of them was the first bad one, and it ends with a list of candidates.

beats.text: Forgetting git bisect reset. Root cause: until the reset, HEAD is detached, and commits made in that state belong to no branch.
